summary: History/ELA topic for ages 7–9: the 1911 race to the South Pole (Amundsen vs Scott) and Shackleton's 1914 Endurance expedition. The learning goal moves beyond 'who won' to WHY — comparing decisions (dog sleds vs man-hauling, supply depots, number of men, single vs mixed goals) and their life-and-death consequences, meeting the explorers as real people making hard choices, and reframing 'success' through Shackleton, who never reached his goal yet brought every man home. Scott's death should be handled with age-appropriate honesty and gravity.
misconceptions: Amundsen won simply by luck — his dogs, skiing, depots and focused planning were decisive choices
Scott failed because he was weak — fine margins, method choices and brutal conditions, not cowardice, doomed his return
Shackleton reached the Pole — he never did; his fame is for saving every man after disaster
Man-hauling sledges was just as good as using dogs — it exhausted Scott's team and cost precious time and strength
These are legends/stories — they are documented real expeditions with diaries and photographs

activities.title: In the explorer's own voice: asking 'why'
steps: Take on the role of a questioner interviewing each explorer, in turn, about the choices they made.
Ask Amundsen why he brought dogs and laid so many supply depots, and listen for his reasoning about margins, speed and safety.
Ask a member of Scott's party what man-hauling a sledge for hundreds of miles did to the team's strength and time.
Ask Shackleton how he decided to leave most of his men on Elephant Island and sail a small lifeboat roughly 800 miles across stormy sea to South Georgia.
Push back with a challenge such as 'Why not turn around?' and consider the in-character reply.
After each exchange, write or say one sentence naming the decision and the consequence it produced.
activities.insight: The outcomes of the expeditions were shaped by choices and character, not just luck; leading well (Shackleton bringing every man of the Endurance crew home) can be a form of greatness distinct from reaching a goal.

activities.title: Plan your own expedition: decisions with consequences
steps: Choose transport (dog sleds vs ponies/man-hauling), where to place supply depots, and how many people to take.
State your single clear goal or a mixed goal (race plus science) and predict how that choice affects the journey.
Run or narrate the journey step by step and observe how each choice affects speed, energy reserves and safety margin.
Compare your outcome to Amundsen's and Scott's real decisions and explain the match or mismatch.
activities.insight: Small planning differences can compound into life-and-death results; well-placed depots, suitable transport and a focused goal create a real margin of safety.

activities.title: Parallel maps, timelines and primary voices
steps: Trace a parallel route map of Amundsen and Scott with dates and depots marked, comparing their paths and timing.
Build a decision-comparison table (transport, food, number of men, goals) placed beside each expedition's outcome.
Follow an Endurance photo-timeline: ship trapped → crushed → camp on the ice → lifeboats to Elephant Island → open-boat voyage to South Georgia → crew rescued.
Read short diary extracts and study photographs so the explorers appear as real people, then discuss what each voice reveals.
Sort explorer facts correctly: Amundsen (first, dogs, survived); Scott (second, man-hauling, died returning); Shackleton (1914, Endurance crushed, crew saved).
activities.insight: These were documented real expeditions, recorded in diaries and photographs; laying choices and outcomes side by side reveals the causal links, and the three explorers must not be muddled.

activities.title: Checkpoint: contrast decisions, not luck
steps: Respond to a prompt: a student says 'Scott just had worse luck with the weather — the two teams did basically the same thing.' Did they do the same thing, or did their decisions differ in ways that mattered?
Name at least one decision Amundsen made that Scott did not, and explain how it helped.
Explain why man-hauling sledges could leave a team more worn down than using dogs.
Explain why Shackleton's expedition is still remembered as a triumph despite never reaching the Pole and losing his ship.

Tier A (age 7): say who reached the South Pole first and give one reason (dogs/planning). Tier B (age 8): give one difference between the methods that affected the outcome. Tier C (age 9): explain why Shackleton is celebrated despite failing his goal, and how choices shaped each fate.
activities.insight: A full answer contrasts multiple specific decisions (dogs, depots, polar specialism vs man-hauling and thin margins) as the real edge, acknowledges weather as a factor but not the whole story, and keeps the three expeditions straight.

checkQuestion: In 1911 Amundsen and Scott both raced for the South Pole. Amundsen arrived first on 14 December using dog sleds and pre-placed supply depots; Scott arrived 34 days later after man-hauling his sledges, and died with his team on the way back. A student says 'Scott just had worse luck with the weather — the two teams did basically the same thing.' Did they do the same thing, or did their DECISIONS differ in ways that mattered? Explain what gave Amundsen the edge.
checkAnswer: They did NOT do the same thing — key decisions differed and mattered. Amundsen relied on dog sleds (fast, and dogs could be used for food), laid well-stocked supply depots, and specialised in polar travel; Scott depended heavily on man-hauling (exhausting) and troubled ponies/motor sledges, with thinner margins for supplies. So Amundsen's planning and transport choices gave him a real edge in speed and safety, while Scott's team was worn down and caught with too little in reserve. Bad weather played a part, but the outcome wasn't just luck. (Shackleton's later Endurance expedition, ship crushed by ice, is remembered for bringing every man home alive.)
